para_text: 2.1.8.5 Deficiencies in management of Annual Technical Support for IFMS software Under the IFMS Mission Mode Project, hardware and software were to be procured by DoT. Oracle software was procured and installed at the Data Centre as well as the Data Backup Centre in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. This software had been procured in July 2013, with support period of one year (July 2014). Audit reviewed the crucial function of management of Annual Technical Support for the IFMS software and noticed the following deficiencies- • After three months of the expiry of the initial Annual Technical Support (ATS) contract, in November 2014, M/s TCS submitted a proposal for renewal of the Annual Technical Support for the Oracle software at a cost of ` 1.21 crore for one year. There was no documentation available on record to indicate action taken by DoT on this proposal. • DoT awarded (March 2016) the Annual Technical Support contract to Uttar Pradesh Development System Corporation Limited i.e UPDESCO (a State Public Sector Undertaking) for the period 31-07-2014 to 30-07-2016 at a cost of ` 2.69 crore. The ATS was awarded after 19 months of the expiry (July 2014) of the initial ATS contract with M/s TCS. UPDESCO, in turn, sub-contracted this work to M/s Impulse Microelectronics Pvt Ltd for ` 2.54 crore in May 2016. • After seven months of the expiry (July 2016) of the second ATS contract with UPDESCO, DoT awarded (March 2017) the ATS contract again to UPDESCO for the period 31-07-2016 to 30-11-2018 at a cost of ` 3.30 crore. UPDESCO in turn again sub-contracted this work to M/s Impulse Microelectronics Pvt Ltd for ` 3.15 crore. Thus, DoT paid for 28 months of support but only received 20 months of actual support. • Due to these circumstances, IFMS remained without any formal ATS and at risk of adverse events in the absence of support for the periods from August 2014 to March 2016 and August 2016 to March 2017, which was avoidable. DoT stated (September 2024) that as per the Oracle software license terms, the ATS has to be on continuous basis without any breaks in between and if renewal of ATS is carried out with breaks in between then the DoT was liable to pay a penalty. The Government stated (December 2024) that email in support of ATS by Oracle was provided to the Audit, but the said email pertains to October 2024 and moreover no formal arrangement/agreement for the delayed ATS period was found on record. The response from DoT is itself illustrative of the importance of timely renewal of the ATS contracts and reflected the fact that the delays in renewal should have been avoided. Further, there was no evidence in support of M/s UPDESCO or M/s Impulse Microelectronics Pvt Ltd being actually responsible for rendering the required support during the periods when the ATS contracts had expired, since the ATS contracts signed included past periods on post-facto basis.
CONTRACTOR NAME: Uttar Pradesh Development System Corporation Limited (UPDESCO); M/s Impulse Microelectronics Pvt Ltd; M/s TCS
SOURCE CITATION: Para 2.1.8.5, Pages 18-19

para_text: (i) Poor functioning of Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) at Digha leading to release of polluted water into sea Under the Environment and pollution management sub- component of the ICZMP in West Bengal, a project namely ‘Renovation of Sanitary Sewerage Scheme at Digha’ was undertaken by the Public Health Engineering Directorate (PHED), West Bengal in December 2012. The project envisaged construction of an STP with a capacity of 201 million litres per month at an estimated cost of ₹ 34 crore. The same was constructed in September 2016 at a cost of ₹ 28.87 crore. It was observed that although parameters relating to Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD), suspended solids, Nitrogen, Phosphate, etc. were measured, no periodicity was fixed for collection and testing of the samples. Further, the parameters of the treated water, namely pH, Total Dissolved Solids, Oil & Grease were found to exceed the permissible limits. Further, it was observed the tests for checking the fecal coliform in effluent were not carried out during 2015-20. Thus, even after incurring an expenditure of Rs. 28.87 crore on construction of the STP, the treated sewage water continued to carry pollutants in excess of permissible limits, thereby threatening the marine ecosystems.
DEPARTMENT: Public Health Engineering Directorate, West Bengal

para_text: 4.3.4 Delay in undertaking outsourcing works In view of limited in-house human resources and infrastructure, CGWB had proposed (May 2013) the outsourcing of various tasks to take-up the physical targets envisaged in the XII plan. The year wise financial targets for outsourcing works under GWMR scheme are shown in Table 4.3. Table 4.3: Outsourcing works under aquifer mapping Activity Years (Amount in ` crore) 2012-13 2013-14 2014-15 2015-16 2016-17 Total Data Generation (Hydrogeological, - 16.57 61.86 273.62 390.92 742.97 Geophysical, Chemical, Hydrological etc)- In house and Outsourcing Ground Water Exploration-through - 34.95 80.99 176.61 496.53 789.08 drilling agencies During 2017-18, CGWB outsourced 14 works to various private firms and two works to WAPCOS at a total cost of ` 313.78 crore for construction of Exploratory and Observation wells. Audit observed that CGWB initiated the file for outsourcing the work of exploration (wells) only in April 2016 i.e. in the last year of the XII plan period. For next 12 months 72 (till March 2017), CGWB could not finalise the proposal. As a result, the additional data required to fulfil the identified data gaps could not be generated on time and the targets stipulated by the CCEA for XII plan could not be achieved. Further, only one project was completed within original time schedule. Six works were completed after a delay of 86 to 558 days. One project was foreclosed by the Department and another was rescinded. Five works were still continuing with delay ranging between 92 to 626 days. A total amount of ` 194.39 crore was released for the 12 works as of October 2019. The details of the outsourced works are given in the Annexure 4.1. Delay in completion of work identified under aquifer mapping would delay the assessment of ground water and therefore affect the development of ground water management plans. The Department stated (October 2019) that the total data requirements were finalised after the reprioritisation of areas (5.25 lakh sq. km.) in September 2015 and completion of the data gap analysis. Department also attributed the delay to handing over of sites in phase wise manner as per the clearances received from the State government, non-commencement of works by the contractor, idle rigs for wanting of casing pipes, etc. The reply was, however, silent about the delay (till April 2016) on part of CGWB in initiation of proposal for outsourcing works. The fact remained that delay in completion of outsourced works affected the achievement of targets of aquifer mapping under GWMR scheme.

para_text: 2.1.10.3 Non conducting workshops to PG and Ph.D. scholars The Standing Finance Committee (SFC) in its 53rd meeting (05 June 2017) recommended operating a Central Laboratory (CL) at NIA on Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode. The PPP was executed with the objectives inter alia of enabling exchange of expertise, mobilizing additional resources for research activities and expanding the scope and scale of laboratory services. A work order was issued on 16 August 2018 to M/s Krisnaa Diagnostics Pvt. Ltd., Jaipur (Contractor). Accordingly, an Agreement was signed (17 September2018) with the Contractor to operate the laboratory initially for five years. As per clause 27 of the Agreement, the Contractor was obligated to organize workshops twice in a year for the PG and Ph.D. scholars of the Rog Nidan and Vikriti Vigyan Departments, aimed at developing their special capabilities. Ministry of AYUSH endorsed the reply of NIA (November 2023) and further stated that NIA has recovered all the dues and has forfeited the security money of the Contractor. 8

para_text: 2.1.11.1 Delay in setting up of Institute at Panchkula The Ministry of AYUSH approved (April 2017) proposal of the SFC (March 2017) for setting up All India Institute of Ayurveda, Yoga and Neuropathy at Panchkula, Haryana as an extension institute of the NIA, Jaipur. The land was taken on lease in April 2017. An Agreement was executed between NIA, Jaipur and M/s WAPCOS Limited (Project Management Consultant (PMC)) in July 2018 for Project Management Consultancy services and construction at a cost of ₹ 270.54 crore. As per clause 1.2 of Appendix A of the Agreement, the PMC was obligated to obtain all statutory approvals and clearances, expeditiously. As per the Agreement (July 2018) with the PMC, work was to be completed within 24 months from the signing of the contract Agreement or release of mobilization advance, whichever is later. NIA released mobilization advance to the PMC in August 2018, therefore, the work was to be completed by August 2020. It was observed that physical progress of the work was only 13 per cent up to March 2022, i.e., even after lapse of 43 months. Thus, the work was not completed within the designated timelines specified in the Agreement. NIA did not impose penalty on the contractor for delay in completion of work. It is evident from the causes of the delay as intimated by the NIA that the delay was attributable to both, NIA and PMCs; delay in the approval of concept plan by NIA and challenges in obtaining various No Objection Certificates (NOCs) by PMC. The concept plan was approved by the NIA on 14 September 2020, 22 months after its initial submission by PMC on 20 November 2018. Subsequently, PMC submitted the cost estimates on 17 December 2020, which is significant considering that it took 28 months after the contract Agreement was signed on 16 July 2018. Further, it was also evident that the PMC faced challenges in obtaining NOCs from Ministry of Defence (18 January 2020), Electrical NOC from Government of Haryana (13 July 2021), Forest Clearance (13 October 2021), Environment 9 Clearance (26 November 2021), Tree cutting clearance (01 December 2021), wildlife clearance (04 February 2022), Zoning Plan approval (20 April 2022) adding to overall delays. Approval of Building Plan, Clearance from Fire Department and Pollution Control Board were still under process. NIA accepted the fact and stated in April 2023 that the delay occurred in the construction work of the project are due to the higher time consumed in getting various statutory approvals. NIA further stated that it was the responsibility of contractor to obtain all approvals and statutory clearances, which were not obtained by the Contractor, therefore work was delayed. NIA also stated that the delay was beyond control. Hence, NIA did not initiate any action or impose penalties against contractor/PMC. Ministry of AYUSH endorsed the reply of NIA (November 2023) and further stated that the project is being regularly monitored by various authorities of GoI and Haryana Government apart from NIA. All the authorities are doing their rigorous efforts to complete the project within the timeframe, i.e., November 2023. These delays indicate that there is a need to achieve greater efficiency in approvals for such projects by streamlining and expediting the approval process.
DEPARTMENT: National Institute of Ayurveda (NIA), Jaipur (Ministry of AYUSH)
SCHEME: All India Institute of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Panchkula
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 3 of 2024 (SSCA, Central Autonomous Bodies), Union Govt (Civil), Para 2.1.11.1, Page 9

para_text: 4.1.7.3 Escalation of construction cost of ₹ 36.93 crore due to long delay in construction JNV Darjeeling was opened (June 2003) in a private building on temporary basis and Phase-A construction work was allotted to Rail India Technical and Economic Service limited (RITES) in November 2005 at an estimated cost of ₹ 7.55 crore with a due date of completion of work within 15 months. No work was commenced up to 2008 and RITES submitted (May 2008) Revised Estimate for an amount of ₹ 15.70 crore and same was approved (July 2008) by NVS. Work was started in the year 2009, but it was suspended in the year 2011 due to some disputes between the Construction Agency and RITES. In the meantime, NVS paid ₹ 1.57 crore to RITES (March 2011). The work remained suspended till work was withdrawn from RITES (August 2019). No penalty for delay was levied on RITES as per contract. Later, the work was re-allocated (August 2019) to CPWD with an estimated expenditure of ₹ 42.91 crore. NVS released an advance of ₹ 14.30 crore to CPWD (September 2021) but the 42 work was not started till March 2022. Due to delay in construction work, there was a cost escalation of ₹ 36.93 crore. NVS (October 2022) as well as MoE (May 2023) replied that due to unresolved disputes between the construction agency and RITES, the work was reallocated to CPWD which is yet to finalise tenders. The fact remains that the long delay in construction of work caused cost escalation by 489 per cent of the initial estimated cost.
DEPARTMENT: Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS), Ministry of Education
SCHEME: Construction of permanent buildings, JNV Darjeeling
CONTRACTOR NAME: Rail India Technical and Economic Service Limited (RITES)
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 3 of 2024 (SSCA, Central Autonomous Bodies), Union Govt (Civil), Para 4.1.7.3, Page 42

para_text: 4.1.7.7 Unfruitful expenditure of ₹ 1.54 crore due to suspension of work Construction of Phase - A building of JNV Tuensang district of Nagaland with an initial estimated cost of ₹ 7.88 crore was allocated (October 2001) to RITES. The estimate was later revised (September 2011) for ₹ 13.11 crore. The work was to be completed within 15 months including pre construction activities. RITES awarded the construction work of Phase ‘A’ to the contractor at negotiated bid price of ₹ 3.91 crore. A total amount of ₹ 1.54 crore was incurred on construction of Phase-A work, but the work was yet to be completed. Project was under suspension since 2012 as RITES failed to manage the project properly which resulted in delay in completion of the work even after a lapse of 21 years. Despite the work was not completed within the stipulated time, NVS did not take any action to withdraw the work from RITES for 21 years and initiate penalty provisions on RITES for non- completion of work. Finally, the work was withdrawn from RITES in November 2022 and now they are in the process of re-allocation to another construction agency. Thus, the delay in execution of work for 21 years and delay in withdrawing of work by NVS from RITES resulted in unfruitful expenditure of ₹ 1.54 crore. Besides, abnormal cost overrun could not be ruled out. MoE replied (May 2023) that State of Nagaland has many local issues which provide less time for construction works and makes the working difficult. During the course of execution, a dispute between the contractor and RITES took place and work remained under suspension. NVS has withdrawn the work on November 2022 due to non-finalization of tender by RITES. The allocation of balance work to other construction agency is in process and the left over works will be completed by June 2024. The reply of the Ministry is not convincing as there was abnormal delay in withdrawal of work from M/s RITES despite it did not execute the work for 21 years. 45
DEPARTMENT: Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS), Ministry of Education
SCHEME: Construction of Phase-A building, JNV Tuensang
CONTRACTOR NAME: Rail India Technical and Economic Service Limited (RITES)
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 3 of 2024 (SSCA, Central Autonomous Bodies), Union Govt (Civil), Para 4.1.7.7, Page 45

para_text: (B) Excess payment to security agency on manpower procurement As per order dated 02 February 201725 issued by the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization, payment to a manpower supply contractor should be made only after verifying that the statutory Provident Fund (PF) payments have been made to EPFO, either directly from the EPFO portal or by obtaining payment receipt from the contractor, which can be downloaded from the EPFO portal. VBU had outsourced its security manpower requirements to a Security Agency (contractor) and had made monthly payments for the same, which included the amount of PF contributions required to be deposited by the contractor to the EPFO. Audit noticed that the PF contributions paid by the contractor to the EPFO for the period December 2018 to October 2021 as per TRRN26 details submitted by him to the University, did not match with the contributions shown in those TRRNs, when verified by audit from the EPFO website. Audit verification revealed that the actual payments made by the contractor to the EPFO were less than the amounts shown as paid in the submitted challans. Further analysis of the discrepancy between the challans submitted by the contractor and the challans, downloaded by audit from the EPFO website, revealed that the agency had availed PMRPY27 benefit, but had not mentioned this in the challans submitted to University, thereby gaining the benefit of the incentive which was meant for the principal employer i.e. VBU. Thus, non- verification of EPF Challans from EPFO website by the University, resulted in the excess payment of ₹ 15.39 lakh to the contractor (Annexure-4.2). Reply of the University was silent in this regard.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 3 of 2024 (SSCA, Central Autonomous Bodies), Union Govt (Civil), Para 4.2.3(B), Page 58

para_text: (E) Non-installation of high value network equipment The University procured a high value Active Networking Equipment in December 2017 at a cost of ₹ 4.65 crore, for up-gradation of the existing campus Local Area Network (LAN) which was more than 10 years old. However, the procured equipment could not be installed due to the unavailability of proper earthing and electrical wiring in the terminal points of the passive components, for which an amount of ₹ 28.19 lakh was sanctioned by the University in December 2020, after a delay of three years. Subsequently, the installation work awarded to the contractor, was terminated in December 2021, as he failed to start the work. Due to non-installation of the Equipment till date (March 2023), the three-year comprehensive warranty of equipment as well as AMC31 services have already expired in December 2020 and December 2022 respectively. After termination of the contract for installation of the equipment in December 2021, the University did not make any efforts for installation of the high value equipment which led to the blockage of funds to the tune of ₹ 4.65 crore for more than five years.

SCHEME: Recovery of cost of police protection - Maharashtra Police Manual / Bombay Police Act 1951
district: Nagpur, Amravati, Thane, Aurangabad, Nanded, Solapur, Pune
OFFICIAL DESIGNATION: SPs and CPs of test-checked offices
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 1 of 2014 (Revenue Sector, Govt of Maharashtra, year ended 31 Mar 2013), Para 7.3.7, p. 171 (printed)

para_text: Receipt books for traffic fines were issued and returned without acknowledgement or monitoring.
SCHEME: Recovery of cost of police protection - Maharashtra Police Manual / Bombay Police Act 1951
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 1 of 2014 (Revenue Sector, Govt of Maharashtra, year ended 31 Mar 2013), Para 7.3.8, p. 173 (printed)

para_text: Police receipts were not reconciled with treasury records, and treasuries flagged unaccounted credits of Rs 6.04 crore.
SCHEME: Recovery of cost of police protection - Maharashtra Police Manual / Bombay Police Act 1951
OFFICIAL DESIGNATION: Eight Commissioners of Police and six SPs
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 1 of 2014 (Revenue Sector, Govt of Maharashtra, year ended 31 Mar 2013), Para 7.3.9, p. 173 (printed)

para_text: Audit observed that the State Government raised ₹38,464.14 crore through State-owned PSUs/Authorities as extra-budget borrowings. These borrowings did not flow into the Consolidated Fund but were required to be serviced/repaid through the State budget. Major borrowings were through UPPCL and UPEIDA for expressway-related works.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.1

para_text: Audit found that contributions under the Defined Contribution Pension Scheme (DCPS) were not fully transferred to the designated fund managers for investment. A balance of ₹748.85 crore for Government employees remained untransferred, and the Government also credited less interest than required, resulting in an impact of ₹33.29 crore on reported Revenue Surplus and Fiscal Deficit.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.2

para_text: The State Government had not established the Uttar Pradesh Road Transport Accident Relief Fund (UPRTARF). During 2023-24, Transport Department realised ₹9,082.08 crore of relevant motor vehicle taxes, of which ₹181.64 crore should have been credited to the relief fund. Since the fund was not established, this amount was not credited.
SCHEME: Uttar Pradesh Road Transport Accident Relief Fund
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.3

para_text: Audit observed that the State Government did not create a separate sub-head/detailed head for recording Green Tax. As a result, ₹43.10 crore collected as Green Tax was not distinctly shown in the Government accounts, reducing transparency of financial reporting.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.4

para_text: Audit examined transfer of Central Scheme funds to implementing agencies in the State. Funds amounting to ₹880.92 crore were transferred through the relevant mechanism to implementing agencies during 2023-24. This is an important fund-flow finding because the money moved outside the State treasury framework for implementation.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.5

para_text: A very large number of 17,963 Utilisation Certificates (UCs) involving ₹11,872.95 crore were outstanding at the end of 2023-24. In the absence of UCs, audit could not obtain assurance that grants-in-aid were actually used for the purposes for which they were sanctioned. The report also notes the risk of diversion or misappropriation associated with high UC pendency.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.6

para_text: Audit found 524 pending Detailed Countersigned Contingent Bills (DCC Bills) amounting to ₹3.11 crore as of 31 March 2024. Of these, 510 bills amounting to ₹2.95 crore related to earlier years and 14 bills amounting to ₹0.16 crore related to 2023-24. Delayed submission makes expenditure through AC Bills less transparent.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.7

para_text: Audit examined Personal Deposit Accounts and found balances that required reconciliation/appropriate accounting. Such accounts are required to be properly operated and reconciled so that Government funds are not kept outside the normal accounting framework without proper monitoring.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.8

para_text: Audit observed that large amounts were booked under the omnibus Minor Head “800 – Other Expenditure”, which does not clearly identify the specific scheme/programme to which expenditure relates. Such classification reduces transparency in Government financial reporting.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.9

para_text: Audit found that expenditure under the omnibus Object Head “42 – Other Expenditure” was significant in a number of grants. Such broad classification makes it difficult to identify the actual nature and purpose of expenditure and affects transparency in financial reporting.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.10

para_text: Audit examined outstanding balances under major Suspense and Remittance Heads. These heads are intended for temporary accounting adjustments, and persistent/unreconciled balances can affect the accuracy and transparency of Government accounts.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.11

para_text: Audit noticed adverse balances under Loans and Advances, meaning balances appeared on the opposite side from what would normally be expected. Such balances require investigation and reconciliation because they can indicate accounting errors or incorrect classification.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.13

para_text: Audit observed that departmental figures were not fully reconciled with the figures maintained by the Accountant General. Non-reconciliation creates uncertainty regarding the correctness of reported receipts and expenditure and weakens financial control.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.14

para_text: Audit found that annual accounts of 56 Autonomous Bodies/Authorities were pending. The report states that 388 annual accounts due up to 2023-24 had not been submitted for audit. Without annual accounts and audit, proper utilisation of grants and loans provided to these bodies could not be verified.
SCHEME: Grants and Loans to Autonomous Bodies
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.15

para_text: As of 31 March 2024, 135 cases of misappropriation, losses and theft involving ₹930.86 lakh (₹9.3086 crore) were pending. In 32 cases involving ₹170.91 lakh, departmental/criminal investigation had not been initiated; departmental action in 86 cases was not finalised, while recovery remained pending in 17 cases where criminal proceedings had been finalised.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 4.17

para_text: Audit reported that excess expenditure of ₹32,533.56 crore under 104 grants and 49 appropriations relating to 2005-06 to 2023-24 had not yet been regularised by the State Legislature as required under Article 205(1)(b).
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 3.2.1

para_text: During 2023-24, total budget provision was ₹7,62,484.07 crore, while actual expenditure was ₹5,84,110.09 crore, resulting in savings of ₹1,78,373.98 crore. Audit noted this as a substantial gap between budget planning and actual execution.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 3.3.1

para_text: Audit identified 26 schemes where provisions were made but expenditure was not incurred, with an aggregate provision of ₹9,859.33 crore. This indicates that funds provided for these schemes remained unutilised during the year.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 3.3.7

para_text: Audit noted that a substantial amount of expenditure was incurred during March 2024. In the PWD Communications-Roads grant, expenditure of ₹16,111.18 crore was incurred during March, with ₹268.60 crore transferred to Personal Deposit/PLA accounts in six districts.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG State Finances Audit Report 2023-24, Para 3.3.6

para_text: During 2013-14, Government of India directly transferred ₹9,464.50 crore to State Implementing Agencies. Major recipients included District Rural Development Agencies with ₹4,606.37 crore, Bihar Shiksha Pariyojana Parishad with ₹2,610.13 crore and Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana with ₹725.72 crore. Audit highlighted the need for proper accounting and monitoring of such funds.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 1.2.2

para_text: The Government provided loans to different institutions and organisations, but recovery was negligible. As a result, arrears of repayments amounted to ₹21,379.36 crore at the end of March 2014.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 1.8.3

para_text: The State Government had not established a Guarantee Redemption Fund for discharge of liabilities arising from Government guarantees. The outstanding principal amount of guarantees was ₹1,090.23 crore as on 31 March 2014.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 1.9.4

para_text: A large number of Utilisation Certificates against conditional grants remained outstanding. Education Department alone had 323 UCs amounting to ₹11,994.77 crore and Panchayati Raj Department had 151 UCs amounting to ₹7,125.43 crore. Non-submission of UCs created the risk that funds released for schemes and programmes could be misused or diverted.
AMOUNT (CRORES): department_wise_amounts Education: 11994.77 crore Panchayati Raj: 7125.43 crore
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.2

para_text: Audit observed outstanding balances under major Suspense and Remittance Heads. There was a net increase of ₹21.12 crore debit under Pay and Accounts Office Suspense and ₹66.47 crore debit under Suspense Accounts (Civil), while there was a net decrease of ₹12.57 crore debit under R.B. Suspense-Central Accounts Office. If such balances remain uncleared, Government accounts may not reflect the true position of expenditure.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.4

para_text: Audit examined temporary advances and imprest balances that remained unadjusted. Such advances are required to be adjusted within the prescribed period so that Government expenditure is properly accounted for.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.5

para_text: Against total expenditure of ₹76,478.23 crore during 2013-14, reconciliation was completed for only ₹23,038.68 crore, or about 30 per cent. Similarly, out of total receipts of ₹68,918.65 crore, only ₹55,159.51 crore was reconciled.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.6

para_text: During 2013-14, expenditure of ₹506.16 crore under 21 Major Heads was classified under Minor Head 800, Other Expenditure. Similarly, revenue receipts of ₹433.61 crore under 42 Major Heads were classified under Minor Head 800, Other Receipts. Audit observed that such classification affected transparency because the actual schemes or programmes were not identifiable from the accounting head.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.7

para_text: The State Government reported seven cases of Defalcation, Misappropriation, Loss etc. amounting to ₹11.28 crore to the Accountant General. These cases were pending for final settlement.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 3.8

para_text: During 2013-14, 93 withdrawals amounting to ₹1,141.58 crore were made from the Contingency Fund. Of these, 51 withdrawals amounting to ₹689.79 crore were for routine expenditure such as bonuses, scholarships, diesel, office expenditure, salaries, travel, medical bills and electricity bills. Audit considered these withdrawals irregular because the expenditure was foreseeable.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.6

para_text: In 71 cases, ₹698.13 crore was drawn through Abstract Contingent Bills during 2002-03 to 2012-13 to avoid lapse of budgetary provisions. An amount of ₹264.49 crore was refunded after retention ranging from two months to eight years.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.7

para_text: Audit observed that expenditure exceeding 50 per cent of annual expenditure was incurred during March 2014 under 11 Major Heads. Total expenditure under these heads was ₹1,407.32 crore, of which ₹992.39 crore, or 70.52 per cent, was incurred during March alone.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.3.9

para_text: Against savings of ₹2,419.08 crore, the amount surrendered was ₹2,570.18 crore, resulting in excess surrender of ₹151.10 crore. Audit observed that surrender of non-existent surplus indicated inadequate monitoring by Controlling Officers.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.3.7

para_text: In 80 cases where savings exceeded ₹10 crore and 10 per cent of the total provision, ₹17,311.50 crore was surrendered on the last working day of the financial year. Audit noted that the funds were neither utilised for their intended purposes nor made available to other needy heads through timely re-appropriation.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.3.8

para_text: Audit found that the entire provision of ₹217.90 crore under 24 sub-heads and five Major Heads remained unutilised and was completely surrendered. Four schemes accounted for ₹167.42 crore of the surrender: Frozen Semen Bank, National Agriculture Development Plan, Backyard Goat Rearing and Bihar Animal Science and Technical University.
SCHEME: Frozen Semen Bank / National Agriculture Development Plan
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.9.5

para_text: The Animal and Fisheries Resource Department did not properly reconcile departmental expenditure figures with the figures maintained by the Accountant General. Differences amounting to ₹10.78 crore remained unreconciled under six Major Heads.
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.9.6

para_text: Audit examined the Food and Consumer Protection Department and identified savings and non-utilisation under schemes related to food storage, procurement and supply. The report highlighted substantial amounts that remained unutilised or were surrendered.
SCHEME: Loans for Food Storage and Warehousing / Food and Civil Supplies
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report on State Finances for Bihar, Para 2.10

para_text: Green India Mission ke liye CAMPA, MGNREGS aur other afforestation schemes ke saath convergence ke through funding arrange karne ka plan tha. Iske through ₹10,600 crore ka funding support proposed tha. Lekin ye convergence achieve nahi ho saka. 2015-16 se 2024-25 ke period mein budgetary support ke through ₹1,149.14 crore hi receive hua. Is wajah se Mission ki activities ko expected level par financial support nahi mil saka.
DEPARTMENT: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026, Para 3.1

para_text: Audit ke dauran financial records ki checking mein pata chala ki kai States/UTs mein Annual Accounts properly maintain nahi kiye gaye the. 16 sampled States/UTs mein se 8 mein SFDA/FDA ne Annual Accounts maintain nahi kiye. Teen States mein accounts prepare kiye gaye the, lekin unka audit nahi hua tha. Iske alawa, 6 States mein Utilisation Certificates mein dikhaye gaye expenditure ka amount subsidiary records se match nahi kar raha tha.
DEPARTMENT: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
SOURCE CITATION: CAG Report No. 4 of 2026, Paras 3.10 and 3.11
